meta.description: A flight reservation to support your US visitor visa plan: itinerary with booking reference as a PDF. Learn when it helps and when it does not.

h1: Flight reservation for a US visa
lead: A clear itinerary to support your travel plan, without buying a non-refundable ticket before a decision.
body: ## How travel plans fit a US visa application

The US visitor visa process centres on the application form, the interview and your supporting documents. The form asks about your intended arrival date and length of stay. Official guidance generally advises applicants not to make final, non-refundable travel arrangements before the visa is issued.

A flight itinerary is therefore not usually the deciding document. It can be a tidy supporting page for your plan, for a sponsor or host, or for an event organiser. Our article on [US visa flight itinerary](/blog/us-visa-flight-itinerary) explains how travel plans are treated in more detail.
## What you receive

- An itinerary with a booking reference (PNR)
- Your name exactly as on the passport
- Route, dates and flight numbers
- A PDF sent to your email
See the [sample ticket](/sample-ticket) for the layout.
## When a reservation can help

- You want a summary of your trip that matches the dates on your form.
- A host or sponsor asks for an itinerary.
- An event or tour organiser needs travel details.
- You want to avoid risking a fare before the decision.
## When it will not help

A reservation does not replace a clear purpose of travel, evidence of funds or strong ties to your home country. Those matter far more at the interview. A well-formatted itinerary will not fix a weak application.
> A reservation is not a ticket and does not guarantee a visa. We cannot promise any outcome.
## Return plans

A return flight inside your intended stay is consistent with a temporary visit. If you only need proof of leaving a country, see [onward ticket](/onward-ticket). To compare, [return ticket](/return-ticket) explains the return itinerary.
## Honest use

Never present a reservation as a purchased ticket. If an officer asks whether you have paid, answer truthfully. Never edit a document. Read [is a dummy ticket legal for a visa](/blog/is-a-dummy-ticket-legal-for-a-visa) for the wider picture.
## Related destinations
Applying elsewhere too? See the [UK visa](/dummy-ticket-for-uk-visa) and [Canada visa](/dummy-ticket-for-canada-visa) pages, or check [pricing](/pricing).
## Preparing for the interview

An itinerary is a small part of preparation. Re-read your application form so your answers match it, and be ready to explain the purpose of your trip in a sentence or two. Bring organised supporting documents, such as bank statements, an employment letter or proof of enrolment, as relevant to your situation. Answer truthfully and briefly. Officers value clear, consistent answers more than a thick folder.
## Choosing dates

Do not choose an arrival date that is unrealistically close. Appointment and processing times vary, and the date you give should be one you can defend. Match the length of stay to the purpose: a conference trip should not list a three-month stay. If your plans change, tell the truth about the updated plan.
## Business and family visits

For business trips, the invitation and a letter from your employer carry more weight than an itinerary. For family visits, be ready to explain who you are visiting and why you are going now. In both cases, the itinerary only shows the shape of the trip. Our [visa application checklist](/blog/visa-application-checklist) lists the other documents to prepare.

Q: Does the US require a flight booking for a B1/B2 visa?
A: Official processes do not typically require one, and guidance generally advises against non-refundable tickets before the visa is issued. Check the current instructions for your country.

Q: Should my reservation include a return flight?
A: If you include one, a return within your intended stay is consistent with a temporary visit.
